ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Megaloblastic anaemia is a macrocytic anaemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis, most often due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. It presents with large, immature red cells and can cause neurological damage if B12 is lacking.

sections.p: Megaloblastic anaemia is defined by a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) >100 fL and bone‑marrow findings of large, immature erythroid precursors with nuclear‑cytoplasmic asynchrony.
b: Diagnostic criteria: MCV >100 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils, low serum B12 or folate, or elevated homocysteine/methylmalonic acid.

t.b: Does the patient have macrocytosis? → MCV >100 fL confirms macrocytic anaemia; normal MCV argues against megaloblastic cause.
Are red cells macro‑oval and neutrophils hypersegmented? → Presence supports megaloblastic process; absence suggests other macrocytoses.
Is there a deficiency? → Low B12 or folate confirms the most common cause; normal levels require further work‑up.
Is MMA elevated? → Elevated MMA points to B12 deficiency; isolated homocysteine rise suggests folate deficiency.

sections.p: Severity is graded by haemoglobin level and presence of neurological signs.
b: Mild: Hb 10‑12 g/dL, no neuro signs.
Moderate: Hb 8‑9.9 g/dL, possible mild neuropathy.
Severe: Hb <8 g/dL or overt subacute combined degeneration.

sections.p: Deficiencies of vitamin B12 and folate dominate, but many conditions in low‑resource settings can precipitate them.
b: Dietary B12 deficiency (veganism, poverty).
Folate deficiency (poor diet, alcoholism, pregnancy).
Malabsorption: tropical sprue, celiac, chronic diarrhoea, intestinal parasites.
Medication: methotrexate, antiepileptics, trimethoprim.
Infections: HIV, TB, chronic malaria causing malnutrition.
Autoimmune pernicious anaemia (anti‑intrinsic factor).

sections.p: Patients develop fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, and glossitis; B12 deficiency adds paresthesiae, gait disturbance, and memory loss.
b: Macro‑ovalocytes on smear, hypersegmented neutrophils.
Elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin from intramedullary haemolysis.

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm macrocytosis, identify the specific nutrient lacking, and look for reversible causes.
b: If vitamin levels unavailable, use homocysteine/MMA as surrogates.

t.b: Is iron deficiency co‑existing? → Low ferritin suggests mixed anaemia; normal ferritin supports pure megaloblastic picture.
Is marrow hypercellular with megaloblasts? → Confirms ineffective erythropoiesis when peripheral tests inconclusive.

sections.p: Untreated B12 deficiency can cause irreversible neurological injury; severe anaemia may precipitate cardiac failure.
b: Progressive gait ataxia, loss of vibration sense.
Chest pain, tachycardia, signs of heart failure.

sections.p: Replace the deficient nutrient, treat underlying cause, and monitor response.
b: Parenteral cyanocobalamin for B12 deficiency (preferred when absorption uncertain).
Oral folic acid for folate deficiency after excluding B12 deficiency.
Treat malabsorption (e.g., anti‑TB therapy, deworming).
Avoid folate alone if B12 deficiency is possible – it may mask neurological deterioration.

sections.p: Re‑check CBC and vitamin levels after 2‑4 weeks; educate on diet and address malabsorption.
b: Ensure dietary sources: meat, eggs for B12; leafy greens, legumes for folate.
Provide supplementation in pregnancy, chronic alcoholism, or after bariatric surgery.

sections.p: Other macrocytic anaemias share large red cells but differ in pathophysiology.
b: Alcoholic macrocytosis – no hypersegmented neutrophils, normal B12/folate.
Reticulocytosis – increased retic count, recent haemorrhage.
Myelodysplastic syndrome – dysplastic cells, often older patients, may need bone‑marrow biopsy.

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite deficiency.
b: Serum B12 can be borderline normal in early deficiency; rely on MMA.
Folate levels may be normal if recent supplementation; assess dietary history.
MCV may be normal in mixed iron‑deficiency and megaloblastic anaemia.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of balance or severe numbness
Chest pain or rapid heart rate with severe anaemia
New onset confusion or memory loss

faq.q: Why give B12 before folate if both are low?
faq.a: B12 deficiency can cause irreversible nerve damage; folate alone may improve blood counts while masking neurological decline.

faq.q: Can a normal MCV rule out megaloblastic anaemia?
faq.a: No; mixed iron deficiency can lower MCV, so look at smear and vitamin tests.
Yes, in patients with intact absorption; parenteral route is preferred when malabsorption or severe neurological signs exist.

exam: Explain how you would differentiate B12 deficiency from folate deficiency using laboratory tests.
List the three most common causes of megaloblastic anaemia in a low‑resource setting and the key clinical clues for each.
Describe the neurological complications of untreated B12 deficiency and why early treatment matters.
